cells.tense: The pen is in your hand right now — you're deciding what this week gets to become, not waiting to find out.
cells.ask: Pick one thing already growing nearby and water it once this week, then leave it alone and notice it keeps going without you. Care that can step back and let a thing finish on its own is the kind that lasts, and stepping back once costs you less than hovering.
cells.core:
Things are arriving that you haven't met yet — a habit forming, something small someone's starting, an offer with no shape to it — and you're handling them the right way. Close enough to matter, far enough to let them work. You make room and then you leave the room.

That's not distance for its own sake; it's how tending actually runs. What you've started keeps going while you're busy with something else, and the fact that it does is the whole point. Care here looks like loose hands: attention without a grip on it, a check-in instead of a watch. You get to tend this and still have a life, and most people only find one half of that.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what's arriving without gripping it — and it keeps growing while you're away.
cells.verb: tending what is trying to grow
cells.place: the threshold where what is arriving now waits to be met

cells.tense: You're already living in a week that hasn't happened — bracing for a version of the future and caring for it ahead of time.
cells.ask: Write the future you're arranging for in one sentence, then add the word 'unknown' to one piece of it. Leaving what you can't see undecided for a day is how the next step gets vision instead of a script, and it gives back a week that's allowed to surprise you.
cells.core:
Something's trying to come in this week — a new person, a small opening, a shift you didn't order — and you've already decided what it needs. You're buying the gift, setting the table, writing the lines for a guest who hasn't said yes. It reads as care because it looks like care. But what's arriving can't be handed a plan; it has to be given room.

Done differently, you meet it the way you'd meet someone at the door: you open, you greet, you let them in without rehearsing their answers. That's still generous, and it still holds. It just leaves the thing you're caring for the right to be itself.
cells.sheetLine: You're taking care of a future that hasn't asked you to.

cells.tense: You're standing at a threshold you crossed a while back — the door is behind you, and you're still discussing it as if it were ahead.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest living thing near you — a plant, a message, a half-finished piece of work — and do one thing today that keeps it alive, even badly. Not to prove anything; just to see what it feels like when something gets tended by you again. A thing that brightens pulls you back into the present along with it.
cells.core:
Plenty is arriving at your door — good things, real ones — and you're not picking them up. The habit of caring for what's growing has gone quiet, and it's been quiet long enough that not-caring has started to look like not-needing anyone. Standing back has been doing the work of staying away.

On a good week, this is undramatic. Somebody waters a plant on a Tuesday. Somebody answers the text. Somebody finishes one small thing and lets it count. That's the whole practice: small on purpose, so it fits in a day you already have. What's growing out there doesn't need a rescue. It needs somebody home, and you're the one who can still walk to it.
cells.sheetLine: Nothing's growing because you stopped showing up to water it.

cells.tense: You're already the person others bring things to — it's happening now, while you'd describe yourself as just being there.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you do that others would call caretaking, then decide whether you're still volunteering for it this week. Quitting isn't required; saying so is. One thing put down on purpose shows you where the line is, and a life that matches what you picked feels lighter than one that doesn't.
cells.core:
Something about you is making people hand you their fragile things — their worries, their half-formed plans, their raw mornings. You did not put up a sign. It happens anyway, and you take it, because taking it is easier than naming it. Meanwhile you're running near empty and calling it independence.

On a good week, you're still the one people come to — that doesn't stop, and it doesn't need to. What changes is that you know which things you picked up and which landed on you. Both are still care, and both can stay. One has your name on it and one doesn't, and the difference between them is a sentence.
cells.sheetLine: You've become the place people put their things, and you didn't sign up for it.
